title: The Wild Ox and the Unicorn
lead: The Hebrew re'em is a strong, horned wild animal named in nine verses of the Old Testament, almost always as a picture of power. Modern translations call it the wild ox, probably the aurochs, the huge wild cattle that are now extinct. The Greek Septuagint called it monokeros, "one-horn," the Latin Vulgate a rhinoceros in some verses and a unicorn in others, and the King James Version has "unicorn" in all nine: a classic case of a guess handed down from one translation to the next.

sections.b: Every time the re'em appears, it stands for strength that no one can tame. Balaam says twice of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, "he has the horns of a wild ox" (Numbers 23:22; Numbers 24:8). Moses blesses Joseph: "his horns are a wild ox's horns" (Deuteronomy 33:17). God asks Job, "Can you rope the wild ox to plow a furrow?" (Job 39:10): it looks like the farmer's ox but will never work for him. The psalmist cries to be saved from "the horns of the wild oxen" (Psalm 22:21), and gives thanks, "But you have lifted my horn like a wild ox's" (Psalm 92:10). Lebanon leaps "like a wild ox's young" (Psalm 29:6), and in Isaiah's judgment on Edom the wild oxen fall with the bulls (Isaiah 34:7).

sections.h: How the wild ox became a unicorn
sections.b: The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, renders re'em as monokeros, "one-horned," in Numbers 23:22 and 24:8, Deuteronomy 33:17, Job 39:9 and the Psalms (Swete's edition). It even puts a unicorn into Psalm 78:69, where the Hebrew has ramim, "heights"; Psalm 22:21 spells the animal's name with the same letters (remim). In Isaiah 34:7 the Greek has instead "the stout ones." The Latin Vulgate has "rhinoceros" in Numbers 23:22, Deuteronomy 33:17 and Job 39:9–10, but "unicorn" in Psalm 22:21 and Isaiah 34:7. The King James Version (1611) has "unicorn" or "unicorns" in all nine verses. Later English versions changed course: the American Standard Version (1901) has "wild-ox," Young's Literal Translation keeps the Hebrew name "reem," and modern versions such as the BSB and WEB have "wild ox."

sections.b: The Hebrew itself answers the question. Deuteronomy 33:17 says Joseph's horns are qarne re'em, "the horns of a wild ox," using the Hebrew dual, the form for a pair: one animal, two horns. Psalm 29:6 sets it beside the calf, and Job 39:9–12 sets it beside the plow ox, so it is a kind of cattle. The STEPBible lexicon gives "wild ox," "probably the great aurochs or wild bulls which are now extinct," while noting that the exact meaning is not known. Tertullian already saw the problem: he wrote that Deuteronomy 33:17 points to "no one-horned rhinoceros" but to Christ (An Answer to the Jews 10).

Early Christians read these horns as pictures of the cross. Justin Martyr (about AD 155–160) said that "the horns of an unicorn" in Moses' blessing of Joseph portray the cross: the upright beam rises like one horn and the ends of the crossbeam stand out like horns on either side (Dialogue with Trypho 91). Tertullian (about AD 200) made the same point and added Psalm 22:21, the psalm Christians read as Jesus' passion: "from the horn of the unicorns" meant the ends of the cross (An Answer to the Jews 10). The picture works just as well with the wild ox's pair of horns. In the Hebrew the image is always the same: strength that comes from God and cannot be tamed by human hands.
